To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The BRM, previously thought to be a basaltic tephra deposit, is, in fact, a giant rubble collection formed at the top of a 25-40 m thick, rubbly pahoehoe lava flow.
the Blackfella rockhole Member of the Kalkarindjii flood basalt province in northern Australia is a rubbly pahohoe lava unit, not an explosive tephra.

the Blackfella rockhole Member (BRH) of the Blackfella Creek Group of the Antrim Plateu Volcanic (APV), Kalkarindjii continental flood basalt (CFB) Province, is not a tephra deposit, as previously thought, but is instead a giant rubble collection (15 - 25 m thick) forming an upper crust of rubbly paohoe lava units 30 - 40 m in thickness.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the eruption of the Blackfella Rubbly Member of the Antrim Plateu Volcanics.
the nature and distribution of the BRM, the origin and evolution of the rubbly pahoehoe lavas that produced it, and the implications for volatile release to, and impact upon, the atmosphere.
the nature and distribution of giant rubbly pahoe-hoe lavas and associated agglomerate deposits.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the BRM represents the giant rubbly pahoehoe lava crusts of a series of lava fields that were emplaced at the end of the APV eruption.
the Kalkarindjii lavas are not a single eruptive event but a series of eruptions, each of which has been characterised by different eruptive processes.
the Kalkarindjian eruptions were not a global catastrophe, but rather an important and significant event in Earth’s history.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the BRM represents a giant rubble collection, formed by the collapse of the crust of a rubbly pahoehoe lava, that was erupted in a similar fashion to that of the Laki fissure eruption in Iceland.
the BRM is the product of a giant rubbly pahoehoe lava flow.
the BRM is a product of a change in the eruption style of Kalkarindi lavas, not an eruption style in its own right.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a large proportion of the Kalkarindjii flood basalt succession is not the product of phreatomagnatic activity, but rather a series of giant pāhoehoeflows, the largest of which have been previously misinterpreted as tephra.
a large volume of lava (1,500 -19,200 km 3) was erupted from one source, and that this lava was highly degassed.
, whilst the Kalkarindii lavas are the most voluminous continental flood basalts on Earth, they are not a global catastrophe.
